text: Last lesson's plain split-on-comma broke the moment a field had a comma inside it. This lesson fixes that for good with Python's built-in csv module, and uses it to actually find this dataset's two real problems in code.

csv.reader handles quoted fields with embedded commas correctly — exactly the case that broke the raw-text approach. Just remember that newline equals empty string on open is required for correct behavior across platforms, and every value still comes back as a string, even order_id and quantity.

DictReader uses the header row as keys automatically, so row quantity is far more readable than row six. And this is the real payoff: looping through with DictReader is how you actually catch order 1005's missing customer name and order 1014's quantity of negative one in code, not just by reading about them.

DictWriter needs an explicit fieldnames list, because unlike DictReader it has no CSV to read column names from — you have to tell it the column order yourself. writeheader writes that row first, then writerow writes each dictionary in that same order. The result tags exactly the two problem rows with a new issue column.

Keep these three straight. csv.reader hands you each row as a plain list. csv.DictReader hands you each row as a dictionary keyed by the header. And csv.DictWriter is the one that needs you to supply fieldnames yourself, since it isn't reading an existing CSV to figure that out.

Next up: JSON. You'll take this same list of dictionaries and turn it into a real JSON file — and run into a quietly important catch: quantity and unit_price are still strings unless you convert them yourself first.
